ABSTRACT 1

The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has caused a severe, international shortage of N95 2

respirators, which are essential to protect healthcare providers from infection. Given the 3

contemporary limitations of the supply chain, it is imperative to identify effective means 4

of decontaminating, reusing, and thereby conserving N95 respirator stockpiles. To be 5

effective, decontamination must result in sterilization of the N95 respirator without 6

impairment of respirator filtration or user fit. Although numerous methods of N95 7

decontamination exist, none are universally accessible. In this work we describe a 8

microwave-generated steam decontamination protocol for N95 respirators for use in 9

healthcare systems of all sizes, geographies, and means. Using widely available glass 10

containers, mesh from commercial produce bags, a rubber band, and a 1100W 11

commercially available microwave, we constructed an effective, standardized, and 12

reproducible means of decontaminating N95 respirators. Employing this methodology 13

against MS2 phage, a highly conservative surrogate for SARS-CoV-2 contamination, we 14

report an average 6-log10 plaque forming unit (PFU) (99.9999%) and a minimum 5-log10 15

PFU (99.999%) reduction after a single three-minute microwave treatment. Notably, 16

quantified respirator fit and function were preserved, even after 20 sequential cycles of 17

microwave steam decontamination. This method provides a valuable means of effective 18

decontamination and reuse of N95 respirators by frontline providers facing urgent need. 19

IMPORTANCE 20

Due to the rapid spread of COVID-19 there is an increasing shortage of protective gear 21

necessary to keep health care providers safe from infection. The CDC reports 9,282 22

cases of COVID-19 among U.S. healthcare workers to date (1). N95 respirators are 23

N95 respirators are traditionally single-use, the shortages have necessitated the need 25

for re-use. Effective methods of N95 decontamination that do not affect the fit or 26

filtration ability of N95 respirators are essential. Numerous methods of N95 27

decontamination exist; however, none are universally accessible. In this study we 28

describe an effective, standardized, and reproducible means of decontaminating N95 29

respirators using widely available materials. The N95 decontamination method 30

described in this work will provide a valuable resource for hospitals, healthcare centers, 31

and outpatients practices that are experiencing increasing shortages of N95 respirators 32

due to the COVID-19 pandemic. 33

INTRODUCTION 35

Since the initial cases in Wuhan, China in late December 2019, the COVID-19 36

pandemic, caused by the novel SARS-CoV-2 virus, has resulted in over 2.3 million 37

infections and 160,000 deaths worldwide (2). Throughout this outbreak, the infection 38

and resultant incapacitation of healthcare providers has been of significant concern. 39

Each sick provider contributes to further nosocomial transmission and reduces the 40

healthcare system’s capacity to handle incoming patient volume. One of the greatest 41

threats to healthcare workers’ well-being is the critical shortage of personal protection 42

equipment. Of particular concern are shortages in specialized N95 respirators. 43

The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) recommends 44

N95 respirators for protection from particles <100nm in size, including viruses (3). 45

Across the U.S. and worldwide, N95 prices have skyrocketed and supplies have 46

unprecedented guidance on the conservation, extended use, and limited re-use of N95 48

respirators in healthcare settings 49

(https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/hcwcontrols/recommendedguidanceextuse.html, 50

https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/hcp/ppe-strategy/decontamination-reuse- 51

respirators.html). Effective, economical, accessible, and validated means of 52

decontamination are urgently required. 53

Several N95 decontamination techniques have been validated and approved for 54

clinical use. The  CDC has summarized a variety of methods, including ultraviolet 55

germicidal Irradiation (UVGI), ethylene oxide, vaporized hydrogen peroxide, moist heat 56

incubation and microwave-generated steam (https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019- 57

ncov/hcp/ppe-strategy/decontamination-reuse-respirators.html). The ideal method is 58

one that is simultaneously rigorous enough to provide maximal decontamination and yet 59

gentle enough to impart minimal structural damage to the N95 respirator. Microwave- 60

generated steam is a uniquely promising method because of its potential for daily, 61

affordable, and widespread use. Although microwave-generated steam has been shown 62

to be effective in both decontamination and preservation of respirator function, the 63

majority of published protocols rely on specialized commercial steam bags which are in 64

limited supply today, or other unstandardized materials only available in research 65

laboratories (4-8). 66

Here, as a quality assurance initiative at our institution, we set out to identify an 67

N95 decontamination method that would allow repeated use of respirators. To assess 68

decontamination, we utilized the Escherichia coli MS2 bacteriophage as a highly 69

RESULTS 75

To address the shortage of N95 respirators that are essential to keep healthcare 76

workers protected from SARS-CoV-2, we set out to identify an effective method of N95 77

decontamination. Our goal was to find a decontamination method accessible to all 78

practitioners in our distributed healthcare network, using MS2 phage as a model for 79

SARS-CoV-2. Like SARS-CoV-2, the MS2 phage is a positive-sense, single-stranded 80

RNA virus. Unlike SARS-CoV-2, the MS2 phage lacks a lipid envelope, making it more 81

resistant to disinfection. Due to its stability, MS2 has been used to model disinfection of 82

viruses such as norovirus and Ebola (9, 10). 83

Microwave-generated steam has proven to be an effective method of 84

decontamination (4-8). In seeking a platform with widespread availability, we initially 85

tested two protocols using common household items. Both protocols involved the use of 86

a 10cm diameter ceramic mug filled with 60 mL water and covered with the mesh from a 87

produce bag secured with a rubber band, on which the respirator was suspended 88

directly above the generated steam (Figure 1A). In one assay, we placed the mug inside 89

a ventilated gallon Ziploc bag. In the other assay, we place the mug directly in the 90

microwave without containment. We then examined the ability of both methods to 91

sterilize N95 coupons (excised 1 cm2 N95 fabric squares) inoculated with 107 plaque 92

forming units (PFU) of MS2 phage. The inoculation of  107 PFU represents a higher viral 93

load than any viral droplet a healthcare provider is likely to encounter in the clinical 94

setting (11). After 1 minute of microwave steam decontamination, we saw no significant 95

difference in MS2 phage reduction between the two methods (Figure 1B). It is important 96

to note that both methods resulted in greater than a 4-log10 reduction in MS2 titer after 97

only 1 minute of microwave treatment. The Ziploc bag, however, melted under this 98

treatment and posed the risk of steam burns during retrieval of the N95 respirator. 99

Noting equal efficacy, we proceeded with the open container method of steam 100

decontamination for all further work. 101

To identify the optimal length of microwave time required for MS2 phage 102

decontamination, we performed a dose-response test using 1 minute increments where 103

we examined the decontamination of 107 PFU of MS2 on 1cm2 N95 coupons placed 104

over an open mug (as described above). Following three minutes of microwave steam 105

treatment there were no detectable MS2 phage remaining on the coupons (Figure 2A). 106

To accurately assess the ability of this method to decontaminate all areas of an N95, we 107

inoculated 107 PFU of MS2 phage onto ten discrete sections of an N95 respirator 108

(Figure 2C). Following three minutes of treatment, we observed a greater than 4-log10 109

reduction in PFU on all N95 respirator segments, except the elastic straps which only 110

showed a 1-3 log10 reduction in PFU (Figure 2D). Due to the limited diameter of the 111

mug, the elastic straps draped over the edges, and presumably were minimally exposed 112

to microwave-generated steam (Figure 2B). Consequently, we hypothesized that direct 113

exposure to steam is essential for effective decontamination, and sought to identify a 114

commercial container of sufficient diameter to treat an entire respirator. 115

Ultimately we selected a generic glass container sized at 17 x 17 x 7.5 cm 116

(LxWxH) that had an opening large enough to expose the entire N95 respirator to the 117

vertical column of generated steam. As with the ceramic mug, we secured mesh from a 118

produce bag over the top of the container with a rubber band and added 60ml of water 119

to the basin (Figure 3A-B). We repeated a sterilization time course against 1cm2 N95 120

respirator coupons in 1-minute increments. After 2 minutes of microwave steam 121

treatment we were unable to detect residual viable phage on the coupons (Figure 3C). 122

This represents a 1 minute reduction in sterilization time compared to the ceramic mug 123

decontamination assay, indicating that the glass container is a more efficient 124

decontamination system. 125

We next examined the ability of the glass container to sterilize a whole N95 126

respirator. As described above, we inoculated ten sections of an N95 respirator with 127

MS2 phage and treated the respirator for 3 minutes over the container system (Figure 128

3D).  Only 20% of the sampled sections exhibited residual phage, and of those, each 129

exhibited a 5-log10 reduction in viable phage (Figure 3 E). In one of three trials on 130

separate N95 respirators, there was complete sterilization on all sampled sections with 131

no detectable PFU remaining post-treatment. Importantly across all assays, viral load 132

was reduced by an average of 6-log10 PFU (99.9999% with a minimum of 5-log10 PFU 133

(99.999%) reduction. These results indicate that open container treatment is an 134

effective method of N95 decontamination. 135

Since it is essential that any decontamination method not reduce the filtration or 136

integrity of N95 respirators, we examined N95 respirator fit and function after sequential 137

treatments. After 1, 5 or 20 three-minute treatment cycles, no damage was evident in 138

the integrity of the respirators or their component parts (i.e. straps, foam fittings, 139

nosepiece). Additionally, no odors were detectable post-treatment, which is consistent 140

with previous reports of microwave generated steam decontamination (5).  Furthermore, 141

Quantitative Respirator Fit Testing conducted with a Portacount Fit Tester 8030, in 142

keeping with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s (OSHA) procedures 143

(12), did not demonstrate any changes in respirator performance after 1, 5, or 20 144

treatment cycles. Across all seven exercises in the OSHA-accepted fit test protocol, we 145

observed component Fit Factor scores in excess of the 100 Fit Factor minimum and 146

overall Fit Factor values >175 after 1, 5, and 20 treatment cycles. Cumulatively these 147

data indicate that fit, seal, and filtration of the N95 respirator is preserved even after 20 148

consecutive treatments. 149

Lastly, post-treatment respirators did not show a significant change in mass (< 150

1mg) compared with pre-treatment respirators. Therefore, in contrast to another study 151

employing commercial microwave steam bags, microwave-generated steam over an 152

open vessel was not associated with significant water retention (6). This is likely due to 153

the fact that the N95 respirator is suspended above the steam and is not in any 154

sustained, direct contact with water. The lack of water retention means little to no drying 155

time is required post-treatment prior to N95 respirator use. 156

In summary, we identified an effective method of N95 decontamination by 157

microwave generated steam utilizing universally accessible materials. Our method 158

resulted in almost complete sterilization after only three minutes of treatment and did 159

not appear to affect the integrity of N95 filtration or fit with repeated treatment. 160

DISCUSSION 162

Due to the rapid spread of COVID-19, hospitals, healthcare centers, and 163

outpatient practices are experiencing increasing shortages of protective gear necessary 164

to keep health care providers safe from infection. Specialized N95 respirators are 165

recommended by the CDC for protection from COVID-19 166

(https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/hcwcontrols/recommendedguidanceextuse.html. 167

https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/hcp/ppe-strategy/decontamination-reuse- 168

respirators.html). Although N95 respirators are normally only recommended for single 169

use, the severe shortages have necessitated the need consistent for re-use. During 170

patient care, however, the surfaces of N95 respirators are likely contaminated by viral 171

aerosols. Recent work has demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 can survive on surfaces for 172

up to 72 hours (13). Without decontamination, N95 respirators can serve as infectious 173

fomites and pose a risk to healthcare providers. In order to conserve supply and provide 174

healthcare workers protection, there has been an effort to identify viable methods of 175

N95 decontamination. 176

The CDC reports a variety of decontamination methods, including ultraviolet 177

germicidal Irradiation (UVGI), ethylene oxide, vaporized hydrogen peroxide, moist heat 178

incubation and microwave-generated steam https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019- 179

ncov/hcp/ppe-strategy/decontamination-reuse-respirators.html). However these 180

methods have significant limitations. UVGI is limited by inherent shadow effects of a 181

light-source, and variability in dosages due to bulb age and differing platform 182

constructions (14).  Ethylene oxide is efficacious in eradicating microbial contamination, 183

but is also a known carcinogen and teratogen, and exposure has been correlated with 184

neurologic dysfunction (15). Vaporized hydrogen peroxide (“VHP”) is highly effective, 185

killing greater than 99.9999% of surrogate microbial contaminants (a 6-log10 reduction), 186

while preserving respirator filtration function (16). Yet the technology necessary for VHP 187

is limited to larger healthcare systems that can afford the required equipment. 188

Therefore, there is an urgent need for viable methods of decontamination that are safe, 189

effective, and available in diverse clinical settings. 190

In order to identify a generally accessible N95 respirator decontamination 191

method, we focused our efforts on microwave generated steam decontamination. 192

Microwaves are ubiquitous and previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness 193

of microwave steam decontamination. To-date, however, studies examining microwave 194

generated steam decontamination have employed both specific and laboratory- 195

generated materials (e.g. pipette-tip boxes, modified reservoirs, commercial steam 196

bags, etc.) that may not be generally available or easily reproduced (4-8). 197

The goal of this work was to identify a widely accessible, microwave-generated 198

steam decontamination method. To this effect, we only utilized common household 199

items. We first examined whether contained steam was a more effective than an open 200

steam vessel. As commercial microwave sterilization bags have previously 201

demonstrated efficiency, we examined if common Ziploc bags might provide similar 202

benefits (6). Although Ziploc-enclosed decontamination was effective, our results 203

indicated that it is a more cumbersome system and containment could be dispensed 204

with entirely. Furthermore, Ziploc bags began to melt when exposed to more than one 205

minute of microwave generated steam and posed the risk of thermal burns from 206

contained steam making the enclosed method less compelling. 207

With additional study, we found that use of a generic glass container measuring 208

17x17x7.5cm (LxWxH) resulted in the most efficient and practical N95 respirator 209

decontamination system. Using this method, we observed almost complete sterilization 210

of the N95 respirator after a single 3-minute treatment. On average, we found a 6-log10 211

reduction in viable MS2 phage with a minimum of a 5-log10 reduction. During 212

decontamination treatments, we positioned the N95 respirator with its convex surface 213

pointed downward, onto the mesh-covered container, maximizing steam exposure. 214

Placement was otherwise made without regard to specific orientation of the respirator, 215

simulating real world application. Post-treatment water retention by the N95 was 216

undetectable, eliminating a need for drying time before reuse. Importantly, this method 217

was validated for use of 20 times on a single respirator without detrimental effect on 218

respirator integrity or fit. In contrast, a recent preprint demonstrated that fit and seal 219

integrity was compromised in UV- and heat-treated N95 respirators after 3 treatment 220

cycles, and in ethanol-treated respirators after 2 treatment cycles (17). Given these 221

findings, decontamination by microwave-generated steam may provide an ideal solution 222

for broad N95 respirator re-use, with minimal treatment duration, minimal post-treatment 223

processing, and maximal re-use potential. 224

The MS2 bacteriophage was used as a model of SARS-CoV-2 in this study. It 225

provided a facile system for rapid quantitative evaluation of respirator disinfection. 226

Importantly, MS2, similar to SARS-CoV-2, is a positive-sense single stranded RNA 227

virus. However there are some important distinctions. MS2 is a non-enveloped virus 228

encased in a protective icosahedral protein capsid. SARS-CoV-2, in contrast, is a lipid 229

enveloped virus, making it more susceptible to disinfection methods. Previously, MS2 230

enveloped Ebola virus, and has been reported to be significantly more resistant to 232

disinfectant than both (9, 18). These differences were highlighted in our present study 233

by observation of complete resistance of MS2 to dry heat inactivation at 105°C for 60 234

minutes (Figure 1B) compared with previously reported complete inactivation of SARS- 235

CoV-2 by 70°C dry heat treatment for the same duration (17). Therefore, the substantial 236

reduction in viable MS2 by microwave steam decontamination gives confidence in an 237

appropriate safety margin for SARS-CoV-2 decontamination and suggests the 238

additional benefit of disinfection of other viruses that may also contaminate respirators 239

during re-use. 240

Our N95 decontamination system uses only commonly available materials: a 241

glass container, mesh from a produce bag that can be found at any grocery store, and a 242

rubber band, as well as a common household 1100W or 1150W microwave. All 243

microwaves used in this study had a turntable to enable rotation while heating (Figure 244

1B-C, 3A), a feature that likely promotes uniform heating and steam production. It is 245

important to note that the microwave treatment did not result in sparks even when there 246

was metal present on the N95, which is consistent with previous reports (5). Our 247

decontamination protocol was validated with a glass container, and it is possible that 248

steam generation and results would be affected using containers made of other 249

materials. 250

We began our study using a ceramic coffee mug to generate steam. However, 251

there were several limitations to this method. Notably, sizes of ceramic mugs vary 252

widely, making this method hard to standardize. Although we observed complete 253

similar result using the entire N95 respirator (Figure 2) where significant quantities of 255

Furthermore, the 10 cm diameter mug opening was still too small to suspend the elastic 258

straps of the respiratory above the mug orifice. This led to inefficient decontamination of 259

the elastic straps, in contrast to findings using the larger glass container. Our study 260

highlights the need to examine the whole respirator for disinfection rather than just small 261

coupons isolated from the filtration material as has been generally performed in N95 262

respirator disinfection studies. 263

Taken together, this work demonstrates the effectiveness of an affordable, 264

simple method of N95 respirator decontamination. Use of common household items and 265

the ability to re-sterilize the respirator at least 20 times without detriment to filtration or fit 266

provides a compelling disinfection method that should prove generally accessible to 267

diverse settings including outpatient practices, frontline providers, and remote clinical 268

settings. 269

MATERIALS AND METHODS 271

Generation of High Titer MS2 Phage Lysate 272

MS2 bacteriophage were recovered from cultures of Escherichia coli strain 273

W1485 using standard phage isolation techniques (19). We added 2 mL of 109 PFU/mL 274

MS2 to a 50 mL culture of E. coli W1485 in exponential phase (OD ~ 0.2). Overnight 275

growth resulted in MS2-mediated lysis of growing cells. This suspension was 276

centrifuged at 4000 g for 10 minutes and filtered through a 0.22 micron polyethylene 277

filter. The filtrate was then assessed for viral titer and adjusted to a final concentration of 278

N95 Respirator Decontamination 280

Decontamination tests were conducted using 3M N95s (Model 1860 Health Care 281

Particulate Respirator and Surgical Mask). Excised 1cm2 coupons or whole N95 282

respirators were treated with 10 µL of 109 PFU/mL MS2 resulting in a ~107 PFU 283

inoculation. When a whole respirator was treated, ten sections were demarcated and 284

inoculated, including two spots on the elastic straps. The inoculated N95 coupons and 285

whole respirators were then allowed to dry inside a biosafety cabinet for 2 hours. Once 286

dried, pre-cut triplicate N95 respirator coupons were removed to quantify viral load prior 287

to intervention. 288

Mesh from produce bags (multiple variants were utilized in this study) were 289

secured across the top of either a ceramic mug or glass container with rubber bands. 290

The mug utilized in this study was 10cm in diameter. The glass container (Snapware 4- 291

cup Food Storage Container made with Pyrex Glass) is roughly 17cm x17cm x7.5cm 292

(6.5x6.5x3in).  Both the mug and glass container were filled with  60ml (¼ cup) of water 293

for steam generation. N95 coupons and respirators were placed outward facing side 294

down, onto the mesh, for direct suspension above the steam (Figure 1C, 3B). When a 295

Ziploc bag was utilized, a 2 cm slit was cut in the upper-right side of the bag to vent 296

excess steam. The N95 respirator coupons and whole respirators were then treated for 297

the indicated time in either a 1150W or a 1100W microwave. Both microwaves utilized 298

MS2 phage quantification 303

Viral load on pre- and post-intervention N95 respirators and coupons was 304

measured using established plaque assay protocols (19, 20). For whole respirators, 305

each treated area was cut and removed from the N95 and processed individually. Each 306

piece was submerged in 1 mL LB broth and vortexed for one minute to elute MS2 307

phage. The LB suspension was then serially diluted, following which 100 µL from each 308

of the phage dilutions was mixed with 100 µL of exponential phase host E. coli W1485 309

cells. This mixture was then vortexed with 3 mL of LB top agar (0.6% agar w/v) and 310

spread on LB agar plates (1.5% agar w/v). All plates were incubated at 37°C overnight 311

to allow for bacterial lawns and viral plaques to grow. Plaques were quantified and the 312

total PFU burden was calculated. The limit of detection of this assay was 10 PFU. 313

N95 Respirator Filtration and Fit testing 314

N95 respirators treated 1, 5 and 20 consecutive times were examined for overall 315

integrity and filtration performance. There were not any observed changes in comfort, 316

breathing effort, or odor between control and microwave-treated respirators. 317

Quantitative respirator fit testing was conducted using a PortaCount Pro 8030 Fit Tester 318

(TSI incorporated).  Testing was conducted in accordance with the definitions, 319

thresholds, and protocols for respiratory protective equipment outlined in OSHA 320

and purge particles trapped inside the respirator. The fit-test entailed the seven OSHA- 329

approved exercises, each up to one minute in duration, including: Normal Breathing, 330

Deep Breathing, Head Side to Side, Head Up and Down, Talking, Grimacing (15 331

seconds only), and Bending Over. The PortaCount Pro Fit Tester calculated the Fit 332

Factor for each exercise, as well as an overall, averaged Fit Factor. Passing entailed a 333

minimum Fit Factor of 100 on individual exercises and overall score alike. In keeping 334

with the operational manual, the PortaCount Pro Fit Tester underwent daily 335

maintenance checks throughout the period of testing, to ensure continuous quality 336

monitoring. 337

Water Retention Studies 338

We quantified water absorption into N95 respirators during the microwave steam 339

decontamination treatment as described previously (6). We measured the mass of N95 340

respirators pre-treatment and immediately post-treatment using an analytical balance. 341

We subtracted the pretreatment mass from the post-treatment to quantify the amount of 342

water absorption. In all assays, there was <1mg difference between the two 343

measurements, which remained constant even with multiple treatment cycles. 344
